Dear Professor Suzuki,
I have been studying your work on the screw function associated with the Riemann zeta function, particularly the shifted family (\Psi_\omega) and the zero-free half-plane criterion in your 2023 JLMS paper.
While working through the shifted construction, I arrived at what seems to be a fairly explicit quantitative decomposition. In particular, for (\omega>0), the shifted function can be separated into a linear term with slope
[
\frac{\xi'}{\xi}!\left(\frac12+\omega\right),
]
an explicit constant term, and an oscillatory remainder whose exponential behavior reflects the location of the zeros. This leads to quantitative versions of the shifted criterion, including an explicit positivity margin when the corresponding zero-free half-plane holds and an exponential signature when a zero lies beyond the shifted boundary.
I have written this up as the attached short working manuscript. The intended contribution is a quantitative development of your shifted construction, rather than a claim of substantial progress toward the Riemann Hypothesis.
For transparency, I should also mention that I used large-language-model tools extensively in developing and drafting this work—not merely for editing, but also to explore derivations, check arguments, and develop the presentation under my direction. I have tried to subject the resulting arguments to skeptical checking, but my own background is in mathematical physics rather than analytic number theory, and I do not regard AI verification as a substitute for expert mathematical review. For that reason I am treating this as a working manuscript rather than a submission-ready result.
I would be very grateful for your judgment as to whether the central observation is correct, whether it is already known or closely related to something I have missed, and whether you think there is anything here worth developing further.
If you do find the direction interesting, I would also be very open to discussing collaboration. I have explored some additional consequences involving Dirichlet (L)-functions and one-sided formulations of the criterion, but I have deliberately left those out of the attached version to keep the core argument short.
Thank you very much for your time and for your work that motivated this investigation.
Best regards,
Edward Baker

parts:
The substance and the tone are right — honest about AI use, modest about the contribution, specific asks. Here's what I'd change:

**Formatting artifacts.** The markup leftovers — `(\Psi_\omega)`, the `[ ... ]` display block, `\frac{\xi'}{\xi}!\left(...\right)` — will render as broken LaTeX in a plain email. Write the math in plain text (Ψ_ω, (ξ′/ξ)(1/2 + ω)) and let the attached PDF carry the notation.

**Cite the paper precisely.** "Your 2023 JLMS paper" should be the full reference with the section: §11 and Theorem 11.1 of "Aspects of the screw function corresponding to the Riemann zeta-function," JLMS 108 (2023). Naming the exact theorem signals you've actually worked through it, which matters most in a cold email.

**Lead with the hook.** The single most interesting sentence for Suzuki is missing: the slope vanishes at ω = 0 precisely because (ξ′/ξ)(1/2) = 0, which explains quantitatively why RH is the marginal member of his family — and connects directly to his own §7.1 remark that liminf Ψ = 0. That's the observation that makes the letter worth answering.

**Ask concrete, answerable questions.** "Is this correct / known / worth developing" is a big ask of a stranger. Two narrower questions give him an easy way to reply: has Ψ_ω been pursued by anyone since 2023, and is there a reason the shifted family doesn't reappear in his Selberg-class paper (arXiv:2209.12832, where ω means the root number)? Also explicitly invite corrections on attribution — that's the thing you most need from him.

**Introduce yourself up front.** Your background is currently buried inside the AI paragraph. One sentence early on ("my background is in mathematical physics; I work in quantum computing") reads better than having it emerge as a caveat.

**Tighten the AI paragraph.** Keep the full disclosure but cut one layer of hedging — three sentences saying "this needs expert review" can be two.

Here's a redraft incorporating all of that:

---

Subject: A quantitative form of the shifted screw-function criterion (§11 of your JLMS 2023 paper)

Dear Professor Suzuki,

I have been studying §11 of your paper "Aspects of the screw function corresponding to the Riemann zeta-function" (J. London Math. Soc. 108, 2023) — the shifted family Ψ_ω and the zero-free half-plane criterion of Theorem 11.1, which as far as I can tell has attracted no follow-up, including in your later papers on screw functions. By way of introduction: my background is in mathematical physics rather than analytic number theory; I work in quantum computing.

Working through the shifted construction, I arrived at a quantitative decomposition: for 0 < ω < 1/2, Ψ_ω(t) splits exactly into a linear term with slope (ξ′/ξ)(1/2 + ω) and intercept (ξ′/ξ)′(1/2 + ω) — both unconditional closed forms — plus an oscillatory remainder that is exponentially damped whenever the corresponding half-plane is zero-free. So every valid shifted criterion holds with an explicit linear margin, while a zero beyond the shifted boundary drives Ψ_ω at the exact exponential rate Re ρ − 1/2 − ω. The slope vanishes at ω = 0 precisely because (ξ′/ξ)(1/2) = 0, which seems to explain quantitatively why the RH case is the marginal member of the family, in line with your §7.1 remark that lim inf Ψ = 0. The same Landau-type argument also gives one-sided forms, including: RH is equivalent to the integrability of the negative part of Ψ. This is written up in the attached short manuscript (9 pages). It is intended as a quantitative development of your construction, not as a claim of progress toward RH.

For transparency: I used large-language-model tools extensively in developing and drafting this work — to explore derivations, check arguments, and prepare the manuscript, under my direction. I have subjected the arguments to skeptical checking, but I do not regard that as a substitute for expert review, which is why I am treating this as a working manuscript.

May I ask three things? Whether you or others have pursued Ψ_ω further since 2023; whether there was a particular reason the shifted family does not reappear in your Selberg-class paper (arXiv:2209.12832); and whether the central decomposition is correct and worth developing. I would welcome any corrections, especially on attribution. I have also worked out extensions to real primitive Dirichlet L-functions (where the criterion turns out to be blind to real zeros, which seems related to the real-zero hypothesis in your Selberg-class Theorem 1.1) and some averaged one-sided formulations, kept out of the attached version for brevity — I would be glad to send them, and would be very open to collaborating if the direction interests you.

Thank you for your time, and for the work that motivated this.

Best regards,
Edward Baker

---

One judgment call to flag: I moved the Dirichlet teaser from a bare mention to one clause about Siegel-zero blindness, because it's the extension most likely to interest him — it speaks directly to a hypothesis in his own later paper. If you'd rather keep the first email maximally short, that clause is the first thing to cut.

parts:
This is worth doing, and I'd say it with more confidence than usual — but only in one specific form, and the project's own notes tell us exactly which one.

The honest starting point is that "RH as physics" is a crowded, low-credibility genre. Hilbert–Pólya essays and phase-transition analogies are abundant, and both communities discount papers whose content is the correspondence itself. Your losslessness theorem (from the one-sided criterion note) is the internal discipline here: we proved that no reformulation — shifting, smoothing, integrating, re-framing — gains an exponent, so a physics paper can never honestly present the analogy as leverage on RH. If the second paper were "the shifted criterion looks like a phase transition," I'd advise against writing it.

But the project is sitting on something better than analogy: an actual, unconditional spectral object that nobody has computed. For ω ≥ 1/2, −Ψ_ω is a screw function outright — no hypothesis — so Kreĭn–Langer attaches to it a genuine Kreĭn string / canonical system, built entirely from PNT-grade arithmetic. The zeta function unconditionally carries a one-parameter family of these systems; Θ ≤ 1/2 + ω₀ is precisely the statement that the family continues down to ω₀, and RH that it reaches the de Branges realizations at ω = 0. The full paper flags this in one paragraph (§10.5.4) and notes no one has done it: compute the string explicitly at and above ω = 1/2, and describe its degeneration as ω ↓ 1/2 — where we already know the window diverges like 0.72(1/2−ω)⁻² crossing over to exponent 5/2, which is exactly the kind of critical-scaling-with-crossover structure that community reads fluently. The closed forms A(ω), B(ω) pin the string's leading behavior, so there's a real calculation with checkable answers. That computation is the paper. Around it, three things slot in naturally: the order-parameter theorem (already proved — this is where the phase-transition, latent-margin language we stripped from the math papers belongs, stated as the rigorous theorem it is); Siegel shielding as an explicit symmetry-breaking mechanism (the real zero supplies the frequency-zero mode that lifts the oscillation — physicists will recognize this instantly); and the dictionary connecting Suzuki's operator realization, Connes' Weil form, and the shifted family — where the Connes note documented that three groups are working on essentially one operator with citation gaps between them, so a well-made bridge has genuine service value and a ready audience.

Two more arguments in favor. The Connes note also identified the cheapest high-value experiment in twelve rounds — the odd sector of the Weil form at Groskin's cutoffs, hours of compute on public code — which would make a natural numerics section and give the paper a result nobody else has. And strategically, the physics paper diversifies your outreach: if the number-theory letters go quiet, the inverse-spectral and mathematical-physics communities (the Berry–Keating, Sierra, Connes–Consani orbit; J. Phys. A or SIGMA as venues) are a second door, entered with an unconditional computation rather than a pitch.

Two cautions on sequencing. The string computation is independent of the margin paper's conditional results, so it can start now without waiting on Suzuki — but the framing sections lean on the decomposition, so I'd hold off *finishing* the paper until the zeta-case core has survived at least one expert read. And the paper must say, as plainly as the others do, that the correspondence transports the difficulty rather than reducing it; given the genre it enters, that sentence is load-bearing.

If you want, I can start on the concrete end: work out what the string of −Ψ_ω at ω = 1/2 actually is — set up the inverse-spectral computation, check it against the A(ω), B(ω) constraints, and probe the degeneration numerically. That would tell us within a round whether the centerpiece holds enough substance to carry the paper.

parts:
The centerpiece holds — and it's better than I'd hoped. Here's what one round established, all unconditional at ω ≥ 1/2 (note saved to the project as `NOTE_omega_string.md`, figures in the chat):

**The spectral measure of the ω-string is identified and verified six ways.** The Weyl function q_ω(z) = i(ξ′/ξ)(½+ω−i√z)/√z — the exact ω-analogue of Suzuki's §9 construction — has absolutely continuous spectral density ρ_ω(u) = (1/π)Re(ξ′/ξ)(½+ω+iu): the zero-counting measure smeared by Lorentzians whose width is each zero's distance to the shifted line. Verified against the zero sum (10⁻⁷), the prime side (10⁻⁷), Suzuki's arithmetic Ψ_{1/2} formula (10⁻⁶), and the Weyl transform (4×10⁻⁷). Two clean identities fall out: the integrated density of states is exactly the Riemann–von Mangoldt count — the string has the Hilbert–Pólya Weyl law — and **the margin slope of the first paper equals π × DOS(0)**. The two papers' central quantities are literally the same object.

**The string itself is computed.** A Herglotz-peeling inverse-spectral algorithm (round-trips exact to 10⁻¹²¹; every production string reproduces its target Weyl function to 10⁻¹¹⁷) yields the structure: a light universal UV region (Kotani's 4x/log²x law, now unconditional via Kasahara duality), an arithmetic crossover where the low zeros live, and a **homogeneous bulk of density exactly (ξ′/ξ)(½+ω)⁻²** — the inverse square of the margin slope. The ω-scaling of the bulk came out right to 1 part in 10⁴ across ω = 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, and after cancelling discretization bias against an exactly-solvable control, the absolute constant agrees to 5×10⁻⁴. At ω = ½ the zeta string's bulk density is the concrete constant (ξ′/ξ)(1)⁻² = 1874.7255…

**The degeneration story is now sharp.** For ω > ω_c the string is a scattering system (purely a.c. spectrum); as ω ↓ 0 under RH the Lorentzians collapse to point masses 2 at γ² — Kotani's zeta string — and the bulk density diverges like (B(0)ω)⁻². RH is precisely the statement that this a.c.→pure-point localization transition happens at ω = 0; below ω_c the measure loses positivity and the string ceases to exist, which is the dichotomy theorem seen from the spectral side.

So the physics paper has a real spine: a computable, unconditional spectral family with explicit constants, not an analogy. The remaining work is mostly writing (the measure identification needs its two-line Herglotz proof written out, the Kotani UV law its short Kasahara section) plus one methodological upgrade if we want the bulk constant directly rather than via the control (the O(n³) peeling caps resolution — a Gelfand–Levitan route would push further). Happy to start drafting the paper skeleton around this whenever you like.
